title: Accuracy, reach, and content quality of information about obsessive-compulsive disorder on TikTok
screen_reason: The abstract reports a verbatim share of items in a sample judged inaccurate against an external standard: of 117 informational TikTok videos about OCD, 22 (18.8%) were inaccurate. Items were coded for accuracy (accurate / overgeneralizing / inaccurate), i.e. judged for truth against clinical knowledge, so this is CONTENT prevalence. The understandability/actionability measures are QUALITY and are reported without shares.

estimates.measure_type: % of informational TikTok videos about OCD coded inaccurate
estimates.denominator: 117 informational TikTok videos about obsessive-compulsive disorder
estimates.definition: A video was counted in the numerator if coders assigned it the 'inaccurate' level of the three-level accuracy variable (accurate, overgeneralizing, inaccurate).
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition; accuracy operationalised in three levels: "the accuracy (i.e., accurate, overgeneralizing, or inaccurate) ... of 117 informational TikTok videos about OCD"
estimates.source_quote: Of the 117 analyzed videos, 64 (54.7%) were accurate, 31 (26.5%) overgeneralizing, and 22 (18.8%) inaccurate.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Researcher coding of each video's accuracy into accurate / overgeneralizing / inaccurate, plus understandability and actionability. The standard used, the number of coders and inter-rater reliability are not reported in the abstract.
estimates.moderator_quote: This study analyzed the accuracy (i.e., accurate, overgeneralizing, or inaccurate), reach (i.e., views, likes, comments, and shares), and content quality (i.e., understandability and actionability) of 117 informational TikTok videos about OCD.
estimates.notes: Abstract only. Country of the sample is not stated (TikTok content, presumably English-language), so coded Global. Data-collection date is not stated; year is the publication year taken from the DOI (10.1521/bumc.2025.89.2.154) - flagged so it is not read as a collection year. Sampling method (search terms, ranking, whether top-N) is not described, so denom_selection is left empty even though a TikTok search is likely rank-truncated. breadth coded 'false' because the strict 'inaccurate' label is the numerator here; the milder 'overgeneralizing' category is recorded as a separate QUALITY row.

estimates.measure_type: % of informational TikTok videos about OCD coded overgeneralizing (intermediate accuracy level)
estimates.denominator: 117 informational TikTok videos about obsessive-compulsive disorder
estimates.definition: A video was counted in the numerator if coders assigned it the middle 'overgeneralizing' level of the three-level accuracy variable.
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition; accuracy operationalised in three levels: "the accuracy (i.e., accurate, overgeneralizing, or inaccurate)"
estimates.source_quote: Of the 117 analyzed videos, 64 (54.7%) were accurate, 31 (26.5%) overgeneralizing, and 22 (18.8%) inaccurate.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Researcher coding of video accuracy into accurate / overgeneralizing / inaccurate; standard, coder count and reliability not reported in the abstract.
estimates.moderator_quote: Of the 117 analyzed videos, 64 (54.7%) were accurate, 31 (26.5%) overgeneralizing, and 22 (18.8%) inaccurate.
estimates.notes: Judgement call for the adjudicator: 'overgeneralizing' is a disjoint middle category, not a broader version of 'inaccurate'. A wholly true statement can be labelled overgeneralizing (true but overstated in scope), which by the governing rule sends it to QUALITY rather than CONTENT, so this row is kept for the record and excluded from prevalence. It must NOT be added to the 18.8% row: 18.8 + 26.5 = 45.3 would be a cross-category sum, and 100 - 54.7 the same complement, both barred by the value keep rule. If the review's convention is that 'overgeneralizing' counts as misleading content, this row is the one to re-type to CONTENT / breadth=misleading, and the two rows then become alternative definitions of the same cell.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) the accurate share, 64 (54.7%) - the complement, not a misinformation share; (2) the combined not-accurate share (45.3%), because it is a cross-category sum / complement I would have had to compute, which the value keep rule forbids; (3) accuracy by creator type - 'HCP-created videos were significantly more accurate (82.1% accurate) than non-HCP-created ones (individuals with lived experiences: 63.6% accurate; others: 35.7%)' - these are subgroup shares of ACCURATE videos with unstated subgroup denominators, and subgroup rows are not the paper's headline, so they are left out (an adjudicator wanting a creator-type moderator would need the full text for the denominators); (4) reach metrics (views, likes, comments, shares), reported only as not varying significantly by accuracy level or creator type, with no view-weighted share of misinformation, so no EXPOSURE or REACH row; (5) understandability and actionability (PEMAT-style QUALITY measures), reported only as 'moderately understandable' and 'actionability was low overall', i.e. no share and no mean, so no row.

rob.design: Content analysis of 117 informational TikTok videos about OCD; each video coded for accuracy (accurate / overgeneralizing / inaccurate), reach metrics (views, likes, comments, shares), content quality (understandability, actionability), and creator type (health care professionals, individuals with lived experience, others). Search strategy, sampling window, country, number of coders and inter-rater reliability are not reported in the abstract.
